The search turned up the origin of the warning and Cloudflare's guidance on setting the date, but no current documentation on exactly what Wrangler does when the field is missing.

- **Origin:** In wrangler-legacy v1.19.3, Wrangler began generating compatibility_date in wrangler init and warning if it's missing. The stated goal was that everyone should specify one in their wrangler.toml. The same release also warns when parsing old ones that are missing it.
- **Narrowed scope:** In v1.19.4, the warning was changed to only occur when using wrangler publish. We do not want this warning to be sent when using other commands like wrangler tail, etc.
- **Recommended value:** Cloudflare's docs say that when you start your project, you should always set compatibility_date to the current date. They also note that there is no need to update your compatibility_date if you do not want to.
- **Why it matters:** Compatibility flags will often have a date in which they are enabled by default, and so, by specifying a compatibility_date for your Worker, you can quickly enable all of these various compatibility flags up to, and including, that date.

I did not find a source confirming what the default is when the field is absent. From my general knowledge, newer Wrangler versions fill in a date when it is missing and print a warning, but I could not verify that here, and the behavior may have changed. Check the current Wrangler source or the warning text itself for your version. The fix is to add `compatibility_date = "YYYY-MM-DD"` to your wrangler.toml, using today's date for a new project.

content.content:
This commit doesn't change the default for a missing `compatibility_date`, and it adds no warning for that case. The new `validateCompatibilityDate` validator returns early when the value is undefined:

> `if (value === undefined) { return true; }`

The `inheritable(...)` call still ends with `undefined` as its default argument, so a missing date stays unset.

The commit only adds error messages for present values that are invalid: a non-string type, en- or em-dashes, or a string that isn't a valid date.

I couldn't find a page that contains that exact warning text, so I can't confirm its wording or exactly when Wrangler prints it. The results do cover the behavior behind it, though.

Wrangler used to default to the current date when a Worker had no compatibility date. A changelog entry says the default for `wrangler dev` sessions without a configured date was changed to the version of workerd that is installed, because the current date could be newer than what that runtime supports (it changes the default compatibility date for wrangler dev sessions without a configured compatibility date to the installed version of workerd. This previously defaulted to the current date, which may have been unsupported by the installed runtime.)

A later release applied the same fix to the `--latest` flag. In Wrangler 4.124.0, wrangler deploy --latest and wrangler versions upload --latest resolved the compatibility date to the current date. Because that date was written into a config file, a date the installed workerd didn't support could break `wrangler dev`. The fix means these commands now use the latest compatibility date supported by this version of Wrangler.

The official guidance is to set the field yourself. Cloudflare's docs say when you start your project, you should always set compatibility_date to the current date. They also note that the new compatibility date takes effect when you next run the npx wrangler deploy command.

If you're seeing the warning, add a `compatibility_date` to your `wrangler.jsonc` or `wrangler.toml`. Use a date no later than what your installed Wrangler/workerd supports. If you want the exact warning text confirmed, the Wrangler source on the cloudflare/workers-sdk GitHub repo is the place to check.

content.text:
It depends on which command you run. I didn't find a doc that covers every case, so here's what I could confirm and what I couldn't.

**`wrangler dev` (confirmed by a changelog entry):** Wrangler uses the latest compatibility date that your installed workerd runtime supports. Older Wrangler versions used today's date instead, which could be newer than the runtime supported. That's why it was changed. In some newer versions, `wrangler deploy --latest` and `wrangler versions upload --latest` also resolve to the latest date your Wrangler version supports, not today's date.

**`wrangler deploy` without `--latest` (not confirmed):** From memory, current Wrangler versions refuse to deploy when `compatibility_date` is missing. They print an error telling you to add one, and don't pick a date for you. I couldn't find a source for this, so check what your version actually prints.

**Uploads straight to the Cloudflare API, without Wrangler (confirmed in Cloudflare's docs):** A Worker uploaded with no date gets the oldest compatibility date, 2021-11-02. That date is from before any compatibility flags took effect, so you'd miss years of runtime behavior changes.

**What to do:** Set the date yourself so local dev and production behave the same. Cloudflare recommends using today's date when you start a project. Don't pick a date later than your installed Wrangler supports.

```toml
compatibility_date = "2026-10-08"
```

(or `"compatibility_date": "2026-10-08"` in `wrangler.jsonc`)

Sources:
- [Cloudflare docs: Compatibility dates](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/configuration/compatibility-dates/)
- [workers-sdk release wrangler@4.124.0 (changelog)](https://newreleases.io/project/github/cloudflare/workers-sdk/release/wrangler@4.124.0)
- [wrangler on npm](https://npmjs.com/package/wrangler)
- [wrangler-legacy v1.19.3 release notes](https://newreleases.io/project/github/cloudflare/wrangler-legacy/release/v1.19.3)
